definition.text: Ecological engineering uses ecology and engineering to design, build or restore, and manage ecosystems that benefit both human society and nature.

facts.text: Howard Odum coined the term in 1962, describing cases where a small human energy input steers large natural processes.
Mitsch and Jorgensen's five basic concepts: it relies on ecosystems' self-design, tests ecological theory, uses systems approaches, conserves non-renewable energy, and supports conservation.
Projects range from restored wetlands to greenhouse systems that turn wastewater into fertiliser, flowers and drinking water.
Applications work at three scales: mesocosms (about 0.1 to hundreds of metres), ecosystems (about one to tens of km) and regional systems.
Design choices should use ecological economics to evaluate alternatives, guided by values that favour conservation.
Unlike civil engineering, which focuses on built infrastructure, it focuses on natural infrastructure and the relationship between people and planet.

title: Ecological engineering functional classes
article: Ecological engineering#Design guidelines, functional classes, and design principles

definition.text: Mitsch and Jorgensen sort ecological engineering designs into five functional classes by how the ecosystem is used.

facts.text: An ecosystem can be used to solve pollution, as in wastewater wetlands and stormwater bioretention.
An ecosystem can be imitated to address a resource problem (replacement wetlands, rain gardens) or recovered after disturbance (mine-land or lake restoration).
An ecosystem can be modified in an ecologically sound way, or used for benefit without destroying its balance, as in agroforestry and multispecies aquaculture.

definition.text: Ecosystem-based adaptation (EbA) is the use of biodiversity and ecosystem services to help people adapt to the harmful effects of climate change.

facts.text: It conserves, sustainably manages and restores ecosystems such as forests, wetlands, mangroves and coral reefs to reduce harm from storms, changing rainfall and temperature extremes.
EbA can stand alone or be combined with engineered works such as dykes, hybrid measures such as artificial reefs, and early warning systems.
Examples: restoring reefs, mangroves and marshes against storm surges; agroforestry against drought; forest management to stabilise slopes and prevent flash floods.
Claimed co-benefits include better health, food and water security, disaster risk reduction, carbon sequestration and biodiversity conservation.
The term was coined by the IUCN in 2008 and officially defined at the Convention on Biological Diversity in 2009; it sits within nature-based solutions.
Many countries cite EbA in their Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement.
It is increasingly seen as a way to tackle climate change and poverty together in developing countries where people depend on natural resources.

definition.text: Although case studies show EbA can be effective and cost-effective, several recognised challenges slow its adoption.

facts.text: It is unclear beyond what limits ecosystems can keep providing adaptation services as the climate changes.
Inconsistent methods and no comparable measures of success make it hard to argue the economic case for EbA.
Governance is hard because EbA spans sectors that manage ecosystems and sectors that benefit from them.
Poverty, development needs, limited access to finance and cultural preferences about landscapes also constrain uptake.

definition.text: Nature-based solutions (NBS) are actions that protect, sustainably manage or restore ecosystems to tackle social challenges while benefiting both people and biodiversity.

facts.text: They address challenges such as climate change mitigation and adaptation, water and food security, and disaster risk reduction.
The European Commission stresses that NBS are cost-effective and provide environmental, social and economic benefits at once.
Mangrove restoration is an example meeting several goals: it buffers waves and wind, stores carbon, nurtures fish and controls erosion.
Green roofs, blue roofs and green walls in cities can cool urban heat islands, capture stormwater, reduce pollution and store carbon.
The term came from practitioners in the late 2000s and was taken up by the IUCN and the World Bank for working with ecosystems rather than relying purely on engineering.
Around 130 Nationally Determined Contributions, 65% of signatories, commit to nature-based solutions, though pledges rarely become measurable action.
A review of 386 cases found NBS as effective as or more effective than conventional flood management, with 66% reporting positive ecological outcomes.
The IUCN treats NBS as an umbrella concept covering ecological restoration, ecological engineering, ecosystem-based adaptation and Eco-DRR.

definition.text: A scientific typology sorts nature-based solutions by how much they engineer ecosystems and how many services and stakeholder groups they target.

facts.text: Type 1 involves minimal intervention, such as protecting mangroves against storms or creating marine protected areas that export fish to fishing grounds.
Type 2 manages landscapes to be sustainable and multifunctional, as in agroforestry or diversifying tree species for forest resilience.
Type 3 manages ecosystems intensively or creates new ones, such as green roofs and walls or constructed wetlands.
The typology assumes that the more services and stakeholders a solution targets, the less it can maximise any single one.

definition.text: Hybrid green–grey infrastructure combines nature-based solutions with conventional built ('grey') infrastructure, which studies find works better than either alone.

facts.text: Studies find NBS improve flood resilience but cannot act alone and must be coordinated with grey infrastructure.
Used together, the benefits go beyond flood management to better social conditions, more carbon sequestration and resilience planning.
Researchers urge looking for synergies rather than framing NBS as an alternative to engineered approaches.

title: Criticism of nature-based solutions

definition.text: Critics argue nature-based solutions can serve as greenwashing and distract from cutting emissions, and that their evidence base is uneven.

facts.text: The Indigenous Environmental Network calls NBS a greenwashing tool; converting non-forest land to plantations can take land from smallholders and pastoralists.
The IPCC warns NBS cannot be an alternative to, or a reason to delay, deep cuts in greenhouse gas emissions.
Of 257,266 papers on natural climate solutions, fewer than 2% mentioned cost, equity or Indigenous and local communities in their abstracts.
Most case studies come from the Global North, leaving gaps for low- and middle-income countries, including cost analyses.

contested_note: Indigenous groups and the IPCC question whether NBS are framed as a substitute for emission cuts and whether they harm land rights.

definition.text: Ecosystem-based disaster risk reduction (Eco-DRR) uses ecosystems to prevent and reduce disasters.

facts.text: It maintains ecosystems as buffers against dangerous natural events while still supplying communities with food and water.
Its measures are often closely linked or similar to those of ecosystem-based adaptation.
The Sendai Framework calls for cross-border cooperation on ecosystem-based approaches in shared river basins and coastlines to reduce disaster risk.
Research has focused on cities in the Global North; more is needed in coastal, dryland and watershed areas of the Global South.

title: Natural climate solutions

definition.text: Natural climate solutions are conservation, restoration and improved land-management actions that increase carbon storage or avoid greenhouse-gas emissions.

facts.text: A global evidence map found 257,266 relevant papers across 22 pathways, but fewer than 2% mentioned cost, equity or Indigenous and local communities in their abstracts.
Canada created a CAD$2B Natural Climate Solutions Fund, including CAD$885M for climate solutions in agriculture over 2021–31.
